subject: An intuitive explanation of AKDE results?

messages.author: 3acab99816f5aedc
messages.subject: An intuitive explanation of AKDE results?
parts:
Hi,
I am doing a study with some collaborators, where we are analyzing home ranges of African cats. Some of the animals show very large estimated home ranges using AKDE as compared to KDE (e.g. 5 times as large). My collaborators don't believe the results - they are not convinced by me saying that the data show strong autocorrelated locations and velocities, nor by me telling them to read specific references, nor by any mathematical explanations. Can anyone thing of an intuitive explanation about why position and velocity autocorrelation can give much larger (and more accurate) home range estimates using AKDE than KDE?

Thanks, Vilis

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: An intuitive explanation of AKDE results?
parts:
Hi Vilis,

Estimates can be much larger than the data for a couple of reasons:
  1. If the home-range estimates are comparable to other animals, but the sampling period is shorter, then this is probably a data quality issue. The animal wasn't tracked long enough to see it fill out its home range.
  2. If the range estimate is much larger than other animals, but the sampling period is comparable and the model fit still looks good, then the animal probably wasn't resident during the tracking period. If you put tracking data into AKDE where the animal was dispersing, then you get a dispersal range out and not a home range. The KDE is also a dispersal range, but massively biased, because the effective sample size will be ~1, yet KDE is assuming the nominal sample size. The way to think about the dispersal range is to ask how far the animal would travel if it dispersed again, but you don't necessarily assume that the animal will continue to disperse forever. I also would not group or average home-range and dispersal-range estimates together. I'm working on tools for clustering and aggregation right now.
If the fit doesn't look good, with matching asymptotes, then there could be other things happening, and many of those things are the result of the animal not having a stable home range over the entire period of the data. Typically when people estimate home ranges they input tracking data into an estimator that assumes IID data with little regard to whether or not those assumptions are met, and the animal doesn't necessarily have a home range. KDE will not give you any indication that these are not good assumptions.

Best,
Chris
